proposal.changeSummary: Corrected the deviantArt/Alexa comparison to remove the dated, volatile traffic claim in favor of the accurate structural point about protocol-level indifference to institutional legitimacy (distinguishing that from platform-level distinctions like verification and paid promotion). Refined the Shakespeare/"community knowledge" claim to avoid overstating the loss of common reference, framing it instead as a loss of self-enforcing normative deference. Tightened the E.L. James/Fifty Shades example to show porousness (via the legal/editorial "filing off" gate) rather than equivalence between fan fiction and mainstream publishing. Corrected the fanlore.org citation to avoid the unverified "dozens of Star Trek fan sites" claim, reframing it as evidence of density and historical layering. Sharpened the Kinkade paragraph to mark his community as company-organized/consumer rather than a Jenkins-style reciprocal-production community, and noted the licensed/developer-built housing development. Added fund entries capturing durable clarifications developed in dialogue (formal equality vs. prestige; contact without a common tribunal; metrics vs. tribunals; universal eligibility vs. equal success; Lanier's sharper platform-incentive worry) that enrich but need not burden the main spine.

entry.title: Formal equality of address vs. equality of prestige
entry.markdown: The claim that the Met and deviantArt have "the same status" on the Web is a claim about formal equality of address, not equality of prestige, institutional authority, or curatorial legitimacy. The underlying protocol and browser — HTTP, the URL, the render engine — carry no encoding of cultural legitimacy: a browser has no field for "institutional standing." That is compatible with unequal traffic, unequal institutional backing, and unequal cultural capital persisting at every other level. Platforms built on top of that protocol layer, by contrast, routinely reintroduce distinctions of their own — verification badges, featured placement, paid promotion, recommendation weighting, moderation privileges — for commercial or governance purposes, not critical ones. What is genuinely new is not the disappearance of hierarchy but the removal of any architectural necessity for a single vertical ranking across communities.
entry.useWhen: A reader assumes the essay claims digital media flattened prestige outright, or objects that platforms obviously do rank and differentiate content.

fundOperations.rationale: The exchange (turns 1-10) produced a precise and durable distinction between protocol-level indifference and platform-level differentiation that clarifies the opening claim without requiring spine-level elaboration for every reader.

entry.title: Contact without a common tribunal
entry.markdown: The collapse of a single cultural hierarchy does not mean communities are sealed off from one another. Recommendation algorithms, trending lists, hashtags, and shared platforms constantly produce contact between communities — fan fiction next to literary prize coverage, a meme beside a museum acquisition. What has disappeared is not contact but a common tribunal: a widely credible authority capable of resolving such collisions into an agreed ranking of relative cultural worth. Communities can see, borrow from, and even feud with one another without that activity generating agreement about whose practice matters more. Markets and platform metrics do generate cross-community rankings, but of attention, clicks, or revenue — quantities indifferent to the internal standards by which a community judges its own work's excellence.
entry.useWhen: A reader argues that platforms clearly do connect or rank communities against each other, seemingly contradicting a picture of sealed-off horizontal proliferation.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 3-8 converge on a genuinely sharper formulation ("contact without a common tribunal") distinguishing adjudication of worth from mere contact or metric-based ranking; this is a durable conceptual refinement worth preserving for readers who raise the same objection.

entry.title: Universal eligibility to create vs. equal artistic success
entry.markdown: Two claims must be kept distinct: that creative expression is now a widely distributed capacity requiring no external gatekeeper's permission to attempt, and that every instance of expression thereby succeeds as art. Fan fiction archives and sites like deviantArt are often ferocious about internal quality: beta-reading conventions, canon-compliance tagging, comment cultures distinguishing craft from sloppiness, informal rankings of essential versus merely prolific authors. What has disappeared is not evaluation but the single external tribunal that once claimed authority to rank one community's best output against every other community's on one shared scale. "No single standard, no community central to all of culture" should not be misread as "no standards at all" — a misreading that critics of DIY culture sometimes need in order to make their diagnosis seem urgent, but which the communities themselves, on inspection, do not practice. A sharper version of that critique instead asks how platform incentives (algorithmic amplification, engagement metrics) can favor certain participation regardless of a community's own internal standards, potentially overriding the practical force of rigorous local judgment without ever refuting it.
entry.useWhen: A reader takes the essay's account of creativity-as-eligibility to imply that all output is equally valued within participatory communities, or objects that this makes evaluation disappear.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 19-22 establish a genuinely important and non-obvious distinction (eligibility vs. success; internal rigor vs. platform-distorted visibility) that refines the chapter's central claim about creativity without needing to lengthen the spine itself, since the spine's existing formulation already gestures at this without the sharper articulation.

spineUpdates.markdown:
As we have said, the development of digital media did not cause the
breakdown of the hierarchy of art and other high cultural forms. The two
happened in parallel after the Second World War, and indeed by the time
the major digital media (videogames, the personal computer, the World
Wide Web, mobile phones and tablets) were developed, the breakdown of
hierarchy was unavoidable. But digital media have been developed in a
way that provides an ideal framework for the plenitude of forms that
have arisen out of the fragments of modernist culture. Producers,
designers, and programmers have fashioned these technologies into a
fluid environment in which all sorts of practices are possible and
equally legitimate. The underlying protocol and browser relation --
the address, the fetch, the render -- do not encode cultural legitimacy:
the official web page for the Metropolitan Museum and a page on
deviantArt are equally addressable, and the architecture that serves
them makes no distinction between institutional and amateur production.
That formal equality of address coexists with sharply unequal traffic,
institutional backing, and cultural capital; particular platforms, for
their own commercial and administrative purposes, routinely reintroduce
distinctions of visibility and standing that the underlying architecture
does not itself contain. The Web with its social media often accessed by
mobile technology now constitutes the matrix for today's communities of
expression and participation.
spineUpdates.rationale: The reader (turns 1, 9-10) correctly identified that the specific Alexa-based traffic claim was dated, volatile, and conflated two distinct layers: the protocol's indifference to institutional legitimacy versus platforms' active reintroduction of distinctions (verification, paid promotion, recommendation weighting). The guide's own refined formulation in turn 10 is durable and factually more careful; the spine is corrected to state the structural point accurately without resting on an unverifiable, now-obsolete metric.

spineUpdates.markdown:
None of this knowledge is canonical in the traditional sense. It may be
intricate knowledge about the Starship Enterprise or the customs of
Wookies or the backstory of minor characters in the Harry Potter novels.
Although most people, if pressed, might still maintain that knowing
*Hamlet* or *Macbeth* is more important than knowing Voldemort's seven
horcruxes, in practice, Shakespeare's claim to commonness is no longer
self-enforcing: schools still teach him and theaters still stage him,
but broad institutional circulation no longer automatically yields a
verdict that everyone owes him deference, or that ignorance of him is a
deficiency needing no further justification. Canonical knowledge
increasingly functions as community knowledge rather than knowledge
that is simply common. Jenkins's description could be applied to the
whole cultural plenitude today, but he was thinking in particular of
those interest groups that function in and through fan culture. The
common intellectual enterprises he is referring to might include an
archive of fan fiction that recycles the characters and situations of
popular fictive universes of Star Wars, Star Trek, Twilight, Harry
Potter, Anne Rice Vampire novels, and so on. Alexandra Alter catalogues
these and more examples in an article in the *Wall Street Journal
Online* entitled "The Weird World of Fan Fiction*,"* pointing out:
"They\'re amateur writers---with millions of readers. After years in the
shadows, they\'re starting to break into the mainstream" (Alter 2012).
She notes that the erotic novelist E.L. James wrote fan fiction before
producing the print bestseller *Fifty Shades of Gray*, though the
manuscript had to be filed off from its Twilight origins -- stripped of
the specific characters and copyrighted material -- before it could pass
through the acquisition, editing, and distribution machinery of
conventional publishing, a gate few fan works cross. The example
therefore shows porousness between communities rather than their
equivalence: a work can originate entirely within one community's
practice and later migrate into another community's institutional
channels once altered to meet that channel's requirements. In the
plenitude of digital media, however, there is nothing particularly weird
about fan fiction. It is produced by a series of networked communities
that taken together, as Alter recognizes, have millions of readers. What
the article refers to as the "main stream" is simply the community of
readers of print fiction by established publishing houses, with its own
continuing gatekeeping and distribution power. Many of the readers of
James's "mainstream" novels will also be reading them as e-books.
spineUpdates.rationale: The reader (turns 11-14) identified two genuine overstatements: the flat claim that Shakespeare has "become community knowledge rather than common knowledge" understates his continuing institutional circulation, and the James example, left as originally worded, understated the legal and editorial gatekeeping fan fiction had to pass through to reach mainstream publishing. Both corrections are accepted refinements of durable claims made confidently in the spine, not mere expressions of persisting disagreement, and both are compressed rather than expanded at length to preserve proportion.

spineUpdates.markdown:
The established communities of art and culture of the past have changed
comparatively slowly. Even the avant-gardes of twentieth century with
their rhetoric of revolution needed years or decades to break into and
partly redefine the mainstream of the visual arts. For example, the
important serial composers Schönberg, Webern, and Berg of the early
twentieth century are still seldom played by major orchestras. Film was
not considered an art form worth studying in universities until the
1960s or later. But in the digital plenitude today, Jenkins\'s
communities "defined through voluntary, temporary, and tactical
affiliations" can form and coordinate in weeks or months -- though the
development of durable norms, stable archives, and any eventual
crossover into commercial institutions can still take considerably
longer. Fan fiction has an honorable pedigree by these standards, with
an early community forming in the 1970s around the Star Trek television
series. Before the Web, fan fiction was distributed using mimeograph or
copying machines, and the process was necessarily slow and limited. Once
fan fiction and so-called "fan work" moved online -- through mailing
lists, Usenet, dedicated forums, and fan-run archives well before the
rise of contemporary social media -- participation could increase
tremendously, and communities could ramify and mutate quickly. The
aggregator site fanlore.org documents the sheer accumulated density and
historical layering of Star Trek fandom -- clubs, zines, archives, and
derivative communities stretching back to the 1970s, decades before the
Web existed to accelerate their growth further
(https://fanlore.org/wiki/List_of_Star_Trek_Fan_Clubs). A rather
different case is that of Thomas Kinkade (or his company), who
assembled not a Jenkins-style community of reciprocal production but a
company-organized public of consumers around a branded product line:
paintings, furniture, and a licensed, professionally developed
residential community rather than participants generating and trading
their own derivative work. Kinkade's website with its virtual gallery
served as a focus for this consumer community and continues to do so
after his death, and its physical manifestations include a chain of
galleries (stores) and even a gated housing development designed and
built by an outside developer under license. Kinkade's community mimics
the elite worlds of art and design of the past, and it functions
parallel to and independent of the traditional museum and gallery
system, another instance of commercial institutions shaping which
cultural affiliations take durable form. (Glaister 2012; Flegenheimer
2012)
spineUpdates.rationale: The reader (turns 15-16) identified a factual overreach in the fanlore.org citation (the source lists fan clubs, not simply "dozens of Star Trek fan sites") and a conceptual conflation in using Kinkade to confirm Jenkins's reciprocal-production model when Kinkade's is actually a company-organized consumer public -- an important contrast rather than confirmation. Both are accepted corrections to specific, checkable claims in the authoritative spine, consistent with the instruction to fix known errors there rather than leave them uncorrected while relegating the fix to the fund. The speed and infrastructure claims were also broadened per turns 15-16 to avoid overclaiming social-media-specific acceleration and to distinguish formation speed from institutionalization speed.

Approved the "contact-without-tribunal" and "eligibility-vs-success" fund entries as accepted: both are durable, well-written interpretive clarifications, correctly anchored, and non-duplicative of spine content, genuinely enriching future readings without requiring unsupported factual claims. Rejected the "formal-equality-not-prestige" fund entry: it is substantially duplicative of the corrected p01 spine text (which now already states the protocol/platform distinction directly), so retaining a near-identical fund entry adds redundancy rather than value.

parallel to and independent of the traditional museum and gallery
system, another instance of commercial institutions shaping which
cultural affiliations take durable form. (Glaister 2012; Flegenheimer

Participatory fansites, DIY communities like deviantART, the remixes of
YouTube, and the template-bound self-expression of social networking
sites, all testify to a new conception of *creativity* as a synonym for
art. The conception developed from the fragments of the collapsed elite
culture and now includes the making or refashioning of almost anything
from the new practices supported by social media, to all the older
practices of visual art, expressive writing, filmmaking, and so on. This
creativity may be blandly appreciated as universal, but it can only be
evaluated in relation to one or more of the appropriate communities.
There is no single standard, and no community's creative practice is
central to all of our culture.

In recent years writers (including Andrew Keen, Jaron Lanier, and
Nicolas Carr among others) have argued that digital technology is
demeaning our culture and debilitating us as individuals. They have
criticized the effects of email and Google on our attention spans and of
the new participatory world of social media on our creative powers. In
*You are not a Gadget* (2010), Lanier was particularly concerned with
creative expression:

> Something started to go wrong with the digital revolution around the
> turn of the twenty-first century. The World Wide Web was flooded by a
> torrent of petty designs sometimes called web 2.0.... Anonymous blog
> comments, vapid video pranks, and lightweight mashups may seem trivial
> and harmless, but as a whole, this widespread practice of fragmentary,
> impersonal communication has demeaned interpersonal interaction.... A
> new generation has come of age with a reduced expectation of what a
> person can be, and of who each person might become. (3)

It is the DIY communities of remix and social networking that Lanier
believes are so destructive. Like many other digital media critics, he
seems to want to return to a prior state of culture. He complains that
Web 2.0 culture is not producing "artists" like Ani diFranco (Kindle
location 1603), whose contemporary folk music is one of dozens of
popular music genres that have won increased legitimacy since the
collapse of the musical hierarchy. Lanier's own hierarchy of art, then,
contains diFranco, and he associates his hierarchy with the task of
defining "what a person can be." He has inherited from the elite culture
the assumption that art plays a central culture role, but he has
expanded the definition of art to include popular forms that the elites
of the past would never have acknowledged.

This move is common among digital media critics as well as many critics
and scholars of film, rock music, and television, who want to promote
certain forms of popular culture into a redefined hierarchy. They want,
in other words, to enjoy the legitimacy of popular culture brought about
by the collapse of high culture, but to ignore the fragmentation into
various communities that is also the product of the collapse. This is an
important aspect of what I call "popular modernism," which we will
consider in the following chapter.
